items.name: Grab bag backpack
items.need: One adult needs a pack that carries 72 hours of supplies on foot, down stairs and across town, with the weight on the hips and nothing about it that says it is full of supplies.
items.how_to_choose: A padded hip belt that really takes weight and a harness that fits your torso matter most. The Prepared's bag guide says any bag over 30 to 35 liters should have a hip belt, that a basic kit needs more than 25 liters, and that most people end up between 40 and 55 liters. All three picks hold 40 liters and are at or near airline carry-on size, so they also go on buses and trains; a bigger pack carries more and weighs more on your back. Pick a plain pack in black or gray, with no camouflage and no webbing. Check whether a rain cover is included or the fabric is water resistant, and line the inside with a trash bag either way. Empty weight counts when you total the bag: the picks weigh about 2.8 lb, 3.5 lb and 4.4 lb before you pack anything.

qty.note: One pack per adult. Children carry a small school bag with their own water, snack, light and a comfort item.

items.already_own: Any travel or hiking backpack that holds your kit and has a padded hip belt is good enough if it is a plain color and the zippers and seams are sound. Test it: load about 20 lb, tighten the hip belt and walk down and up a few flights of stairs. If the weight hangs on your shoulders or the bag swings, it is not good enough.

safety_notes.text: Ready.gov's basic kit list includes water, several days of non-perishable food, a radio, flashlight, first aid kit, extra batteries, whistle, dust mask, sanitation items, local maps and a phone with chargers and a backup battery. It says to keep the kit in one or two easy-to-carry containers.

The American Red Cross says a kit you may have to evacuate with should hold a 3-day supply of water and food, plus a flashlight, radio, first aid kit, a 7-day supply of medications, copies of personal documents, phone chargers, extra cash, an emergency blanket and maps of the area.

items.name: Water bottle for the bag
items.need: Water is the heaviest and most urgent thing in the bag, and a tough 1-liter bottle is how you carry it, refill it and treat it.
items.how_to_choose: About 1 quart (32 oz, about 1 liter) is the usual size for a bag bottle, and the count of two for each adult assumes it; a bigger bottle is fine if you will carry it. Pick a lid that cannot leak in a bag, and weigh the bottle empty: a full quart of water already adds about 2 lb. An insulated steel bottle keeps water cold but weighs about twice as much as a plastic one. Mouth size decides which filter fits. Squeeze filters with 28 mm threads, such as the Sawyer Squeeze, screw straight onto narrow bottles like the smartwater bottle, and do not screw onto a 63 mm Nalgene or a 54 mm Klean Kanteen wide mouth. Wide mouths are easier to fill from a faucet or tub, to clean, and to drop purification tablets into; Nalgene says its wide mouth fits most filtration devices and Klean Kanteen says the same of its Wide bottle, but check your own filter's thread before you rely on it. The Standard bottle here and the Standard portable filter (the Sawyer Squeeze) do not thread together: the filter comes with its own pouch, so fill the pouch, screw the filter onto it and squeeze the water into the bottle. Only a single-wall, uninsulated steel bottle can be used to boil water; never heat an insulated bottle or a plastic one.

qty.note: Two bottles for each adult and each teenager of 14 or over, both in the grab bag. A younger child's bag has its own small bottle. Two full bottles weigh about 4.4 lb; refill whenever you can.

items.already_own: Any leak-proof bottle of about a quart is fine: a sports bottle, a steel flask, or a reused 1-liter drink bottle. It is good enough if the lid seals when you squeeze it upside down and the plastic is not cracked or cloudy. Know which of your bottles your filter fits.

safety_notes.text: Ready.gov's planning figure is one gallon of water per person per day for several days, for drinking and sanitation. A bag cannot carry that, so the bottle plus a way to refill and treat water is the plan.

For moderate activity in heat lasting under two hours, CDC/NIOSH advises about one 8 oz cup of water every 15 to 20 minutes, and generally no more than 6 cups an hour. If you sweat for several hours, add drinks with electrolytes. At that rate a quart lasts little more than an hour of hot walking.

The National Weather Service says heat stroke (confusion, slurred speech, body temperature above 103 F, passing out) is a medical emergency: call 911, cool the person, and do not give fluids. For heat cramps or heat exhaustion, move somewhere cooler and give sips of water.
CDC says to use bottled water if you have it. If you have none, bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 ft) to make it safe to drink.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

safety_notes.text: The 5,000 ft figure is EPA's: above 5,000 ft, boil for 3 minutes. CDC's page gives 6,500 ft; this site uses the lower figure.

items.name: No-cook emergency food for the bag
items.need: Food that needs no stove, no water and no fridge, and that survives years in a bag or a hot car, keeps you moving for three days when stores are closed.
items.how_to_choose: Lifeboat-style ration bars are the lightest way to carry calories: about 1.5 lb for 3,600 kcal with a 5-year shelf life, and The Prepared's oven test found they hold up to heat. Be plain about what they are: one 3,600 kcal pack is about 1,200 kcal a day for three days. That keeps an adult going, but it is not a full diet. This site counts ration packs only for people aged 6 or over: a younger child gets food they already eat, not ration bars. Look for a US Coast Guard approval number on the wrapper rather than vague claims. Ready-to-eat meals (MREs) are real food at 900 to 1,250 kcal a meal; they weigh about 1.7 lb each, and heat shortens their life (the maker of the Cadillac pick gives about 4 years at 80 F and 1.5 years at 100 F).

qty.note: One 3,600 kcal pack for each person aged 6 or over covers 72 hours at about 1,200 kcal a day. A younger child gets food they already eat, never ration bars.

items.already_own: Shelf-stable food you already eat works for a year or so: nut butter sachets, dense snack bars, dried fruit, canned fish with a pull-tab lid. It is good enough if it needs no cooking, you rotate it before the date on the pack, and it will not melt or spoil in a warm cabinet.

safety_notes.text: Ready.gov's basic kit calls for at least a several-day supply of non-perishable food and, separately, one gallon of water per person per day. Food bars do not replace water.
The Red Cross advises a 3-day supply of non-perishable, easy-to-prepare food for evacuation and a 2-week supply at home.
safety_notes.source_title: What Do You Need In a Survival Kit

items.name: Packable rain protection
items.need: Getting soaked on a long walk in cool weather is how people get dangerously cold, so each person needs a waterproof layer that lives in the bag.
items.how_to_choose: A poncho is cheap, covers you and a small pack, and vents well, but flaps in wind between tall buildings. A light rain jacket packs into its own pocket and blocks wind too; the lightest ones wet through in hours of steady rain. A 3-layer shell keeps working in an all-day downpour and lasts for years. Choose a plain dark color, size it to fit over a warm layer, and note that jackets come in men's and women's cuts.

qty.note: One per person, sized to fit over a sweater or fleece. Children need their own size.

items.already_own: Any waterproof jacket with a hood that you already own is fine. Test it in the shower for five minutes over a dry T-shirt: if the shoulders stay dry and the hood stays on, it is good enough. A shower-proof fashion coat or an umbrella alone is not.

safety_notes.text: CDC warns that hypothermia can happen even at cool temperatures above 40 F if a person becomes chilled from rain, sweat or cold water. Signs in adults include shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness.

CDC's first aid for hypothermia: treat it as an emergency, get the person into a warm room or shelter, remove wet clothing, and warm the center of the body first (chest, neck, head and groin). A body temperature below 95 F needs medical help at once.

items.name: Emergency blanket or bivvy
items.need: If you are stuck overnight in a stairwell, a station or an unheated shelter, a windproof heat-reflecting layer the size of a fist can keep a cold night from becoming a medical emergency.
items.how_to_choose: Know the limits. A reflective blanket only bounces back the heat your body radiates and blocks wind and rain; it has no insulation of its own, so it does nothing against a cold floor. Sit or lie on a bag, cardboard or spare clothes. The film does not breathe, so your sweat condenses inside and can leave you damp. A bivvy sack is the same film as a bag, which stops drafts and is much warmer than a loose sheet. A breathable bivvy lets moisture out, can be reused many times, and reflects less heat. Avoid the thinnest silver sheets, which tear once and are finished.

qty.note: One per person, children included. They add warmth to clothing and a hat; they do not replace them.

items.already_own: A thin foil blanket from a first aid kit is better than nothing but tears easily; keep it as a spare. A light sleeping bag or a wool blanket is warmer if you can carry it. Whatever you have, also pack something to put between you and the floor.

safety_notes.text: CDC says hypothermia is a dangerous drop in body temperature that can happen even above 40 F when a person is chilled by rain, sweat or cold water. Warning signs in adults are shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness.

CDC's first aid: get medical help at once if body temperature is below 95 F, move the person to a warm room or shelter, remove wet clothing, and warm the center of the body first (chest, neck, head, groin). A blanket or bivvy goes over dry clothing, not wet.
The Red Cross includes an emergency blanket in its basic survival kit list, and Ready.gov lists a sleeping bag or warm blanket for each person.

items.name: Merino walking socks
items.need: Blisters and wet feet end a long walk home faster than anything else, and a dry pair of wool-blend socks in the bag is the cheapest fix.
items.how_to_choose: Choose a merino wool and nylon blend, which stays warm when damp and dries faster than cotton; never pack cotton socks. Light cushion suits ordinary shoes and sneakers, full cushion suits boots and cold weather. Buy your real size so nothing bunches, and wear them once before packing. Work gloves for broken glass and debris are a separate item on this site.

qty.note: Two pairs per adult: one to change into before a long walk, one kept dry in a zip bag. Children need the same in their sizes.

items.already_own: Hiking or running socks you already own are fine if they are a wool or synthetic blend, have no holes or thin heels, and fit the shoes you would walk in. Cotton sports socks and dress socks are not good enough.

safety_notes.text: Ready.gov's additional supplies list includes a complete change of clothing suited to your climate and sturdy shoes, and it advises keeping comfortable walking shoes at work.
CDC notes that hypothermia can set in above 40 F when a person is chilled by rain, sweat or cold water, and that removing wet clothing is part of first aid. Dry socks are part of staying warm.

items.name: Keychain or pocket light
items.need: Stairwells, tunnels and streets go dark in a power cut, and a phone flashlight drains the battery you need for calls and maps.
items.how_to_choose: The best light is the one already on your keys or in your pocket. A single-AAA light runs on batteries you can buy or borrow anywhere and keeps for years with a lithium or fresh alkaline cell. A USB-C light recharges from the same cable and power bank as your phone but must be topped up every few months. About 100 lumens is plenty for stairs; more output mostly shortens runtime. Look for a water resistance rating, and a way to stop it switching on in a pocket.

qty.note: One per adult, for the small kit at work (X2-07). This is in addition to the headlamp in the grab bag.

items.already_own: Any small flashlight you already carry is fine if it lights when you test it today, has a fresh or charged battery, and survives a splash. A phone flashlight alone is not good enough, because the phone is also your map and your link to family.

safety_notes.text: Ready.gov lists a flashlight and extra batteries in its basic disaster supplies kit, along with a phone with chargers and a backup battery.
The Red Cross survival kit list also includes a flashlight and extra batteries.

items.name: Paper map and baseplate compass
items.need: When phone networks are down or the battery is flat, a paper street map and a compass still tell you which way home is.
items.how_to_choose: The map matters most, and it has to be of your own city, so it cannot be one product here. Get a current folded street map that shows your home, your workplace and the bridges, tunnels and main roads between them: your regional AAA office gives maps to members, transit agencies hand out system maps, and National Geographic's City Destination maps (waterproof and tear-resistant, $9.95 to $11.95) cover a limited list of large cities such as Boston, Chicago and Los Angeles. Mark two walking routes home and keep the map in a zip bag. For the compass, a clear baseplate model from an established maker is enough: in a street grid you only need to find north and hold a direction. Adjustable declination and a sighting mirror, as on the Cadillac pick, matter if your way home could leave the streets for open country.

qty.note: One compass and one marked-up street map per adult bag.

items.already_own: Any liquid-filled baseplate compass from a known maker is fine if the needle swings freely, settles quickly and has no large bubble. Check it against a street you know runs north. A button compass on a zip pull or a phone app alone is not good enough. A free transit or tourist street map is fine if it covers your whole route home.

The Red Cross survival kit list includes maps of the area and written family and emergency contact information.
